result.question:
Continue and complete the VERIFIED citation base for the introduction of a concise Radiology: Artificial Intelligence paper. Thesis: hospitals with surgical navigation (tracker registered to a preoperative/intraoperative 3-D scan) localise the vertebral level instrumentally; hospitals without it count vertebrae by hand across successive C-arm shots; a navigation built entirely from OR C-arm shots would close the gap. The reader is a neurosurgeon who also knows AI, so every sentence must carry a verified number.

ALREADY VERIFIED / IN THE BIBLIOGRAPHY (do NOT re-research; only extend): mody2008 (1 in 3,110; 50% of surgeons), groff2013, furuya2026 (0.12% registry, thoracic 0.42%), longo2012, devine2010, hsiang2011 (level counting; navigation not available everywhere), mayer2008, strong2021, jc2024, kwaan2006 (62% preventable), stahel2010, nhse2025, mehtsun2013, matthews2007, keil2024, mongardi2021, tan2023, siminski2023, childers2018, goodkin2004, machin2018, bettis2026, manbachi2018 + otake2012 (LevelCheck requires a preoperative CT/MR), ammerman2006 (15% initial wrong exposure), upadhyaya2012 (fiducial cost-effectiveness, UCSF), Macki 2014 (fiducial $1,237.55 fluoro / $1,267.03 CT vs vertebroplasty marking $3,195), desilva2018, levelcheck2012/2016, unberath2018/2019 (DeepDRR), grupp2020 (DeepFluoro), synthex2023, fluorosam2025, kwak2025, sxstitch2024, spineclue2024, vertxnet2024.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING, each with DOI/PMID, the exact quoted sentence, and where the number sits (table/figure/page):
1. UPADHYAYA 2012 (J Neurosurg Spine 16:280-284): the exact cost figures and conclusion wording — cost per patient of preoperative percutaneous fiducial placement, the comparison arm (intraoperative fluoroscopic localisation time / cost), the number of patients, and whether wrong-level events changed. Quote the abstract's Results and Conclusions sentences verbatim.
2. NAVIGATION ACCESS DISPARITY: verified capital cost figures for (a) Medtronic O-arm + StealthStation, (b) Brainlab Airo/Cirq/Loop-X, (c) Globus ExcelsiusGPS, (d) 7D Surgical, from peer-reviewed cost-effectiveness or health-technology-assessment papers (e.g., Dea 2016 Spine J cost-effectiveness of navigation; Al-Khouja 2015; Sanborn 2012; Malham 2022; Fichtner 2019; NICE/HTA reports), and the share of hospitals or spine surgeons with navigation access from surveys (AO Spine Global Spine Care survey, NASS/CNS surveys, Härtl 2013 "Worldwide survey on the use of navigation in spine surgery" World Neurosurg — quote its percentages; Lee 2020/2023 updates; rural vs urban US, LMIC).
3. ANY published system that names or counts vertebral levels on real intraoperative fluoroscopy WITHOUT a 3-D scan (no preoperative CT/MRI, no tracker): search "vertebra level identification fluoroscopy deep learning", "C-arm level localization neural network", "intraoperative radiograph vertebra labeling registration-free", 2018–2026. For each: modality, whether a 3-D scan was needed, the reported accuracy and its metric, and whether it was tested on real fluoroscopy. If none exists, state that explicitly with the searches performed.
4. RSNA Radiology: Artificial Intelligence current author instructions (2025/2026): Original Research word limit, abstract structure and limit, key points, figure/table limits, CLAIM 2024 requirement, data/code sharing statement requirements, page/reference limits. Quote the instruction page.
5. The C-arm exposure counts / time / dose consumed by manual fluoroscopic level localisation in the OR (any prospective measurement: number of shots, minutes, mGy or DAP per localisation), to size the problem quantitatively.

Return a structured report per item with the citation, the quoted passage, the number, confidence, and what could not be verified.
result.summary: Four of the five items now have verified numbers; items 3, 4 and 5 are not covered by any claim that survived verification. First, Upadhyaya 2012 is a safety and fluoroscopy-time study, not a cost study. It compared 26 fiducial cases with 26 historical fluoroscopy-only cases and found 0 wrong-level operations in each group. Its abstract has no cost figures and no time figures. The dollar figures belong to Macki 2014, and the bibliography label and the PMID both need fixing. Second, the navigation-access argument is now well supported. On cost: Dea 2016 puts O-arm/StealthStation break-even at more than 254 instrumented cases a year, and Suri 2023 models that 61–86% of US inpatient facilities cannot justify 3-D navigation at about $414,634 a year. On access: the AO Spine 2023 survey found 49% of departments use navigation at least monthly (69.5% in high-income countries against 24.1% in low- and middle-income countries), and in Africa 96.5% of respondents have fluoroscopy against 8.8% with stereotactic navigation plus intraoperative CT. Third, this round verified nothing for item 3 (level naming on real fluoroscopy without a 3-D scan), item 4 (Radiology: AI author instructions) or item 5 (shots, time or dose per manual localisation). The paper should not yet state that no system does registration-free level naming.

findings.claim: Item 1, identifiers: the Upadhyaya fiducial paper is PMID 22054638, doi:10.3171/2011.3.SPINE10445 (J Neurosurg Spine 2012 Mar;16(3):280-284; Upadhyaya CD, Wu JC, Chin CT, Balamurali G, Mummaneni PV; UCSF). PMID 22054637 is a different paper, Adogwa et al. (Vanderbilt), a cost-per-QALY study of revision for adjacent-segment disease with DOI 10.3171/2011.9.SPINE11419. The DOI 10.3171/2011.11.SPINE11419 does not resolve at Crossref or doi.org.
findings.evidence: NCBI efetch returned both records. A PubMed search for Upadhyaya[au] AND fiducial, and one for J Neurosurg Spine vol 16 p 280, each returns only 22054638. The error is an off-by-one PMID. Check the .bib entry for both the PMID and the DOI.

findings.claim: Item 1, design and outcome: this was a retrospective single-centre (UCSF) series in thoracic spine surgery. Twenty-six patients had a 5-mm fiducial screw placed percutaneously under CT guidance before surgery, often as outpatients. They were compared with a historical group of 26 localised intraoperatively with fluoroscopy alone. Neither group had a wrong-level operation (0/26 vs 0/26), and the fiducial caused no complications. The paper cannot be cited for fewer wrong-level operations: with zero events in both groups of 26 it could not detect a difference in either direction. Verbatim Results: 'In the treatment group of 26 patients, no complications related to fiducial screw placement occurred, and there was no incidence of wrong-level surgery. In comparison, there were no wrong-level surgeries in the historical cohort of 26 patients who underwent mini-open or open thoracic spine surgery without placement of a fiducial screw. However, the authors found that the intraoperative localization fluoroscopy time was greatly reduced when a fiducial screw localization technique was employed.' Verbatim Conclusions: 'The aforementioned technique for intraoperative localization is safe, efficient, and accurate for identifying the target level in thoracic spine exposures. The fiducial marker screw can be placed using CT guidance on an outpatient basis. There is a reduction in the amount of intraoperative fluoroscopy time needed for localization in the fiducial screw group.'
findings.evidence: Checked independently through NCBI efetch and Europe PMC. 'Retrospective' comes from the MeSH terms (Retrospective Studies; Case-Control Studies), and 'UCSF' from the author affiliation; the abstract itself says neither. A systematic review (PMC10193475) describes the control technique as needles placed under fluoroscopy and counted up from the sacrum, so 'fluoroscopy alone' is the abstract's shorthand. The control group is historical, not concurrent.

findings.claim: Item 1, the one benefit, which is also a number relevant to item 5: the abstract says fluoroscopy time for localisation was 'greatly reduced' but gives no seconds, shot count, dose or p value. Only secondary sources give a number, 3 minutes with the fiducial against 15 minutes without: a 2023 systematic review (PMC10193475) and the JNS press release on Newswise. The press release adds that the authors call the technique 'cost neutral': the cost of implanting the screw beforehand is offset by a shorter operation.
findings.evidence: The abstract text is confirmed (high confidence). The 3 vs 15 minutes and 'cost neutral' come from secondary sources, because the full text is closed: Europe PMC isOpenAccess=N, OpenAlex oa_status closed, thejns.org HTTP 403. Neither secondary source gives a p value. To cite 3 vs 15 minutes, attribute it to the review, or read the full text first.

findings.claim: Item 1, cost: the Upadhyaya abstract has no cost figure of any kind: no cost per patient, no cost for the fluoroscopy arm and no cost-effectiveness result. The bibliography note 'fiducial cost-effectiveness, UCSF' is wrong. At most the paper supports 'cost neutral according to the authors', and only through the press release. The fiducial dollar figures belong to Macki 2014.
findings.evidence: No verifier found a dollar figure in the Upadhyaya abstract or in any summary of it. The full-text Discussion could not be read, so a qualitative cost remark there cannot be ruled out.

findings.claim: Item 1/2, fiducial cost: Macki et al. 2014 (Neurol Res 36(10):925-927; PMID 24963696; doi:10.1179/1743132814Y.0000000413; Johns Hopkins), verbatim: 'Following 2013 Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) coding, the cost of vertebroplasty under fluoroscopic guidance, $3195·43, or under computed tomography (CT) guidance, $3232·54, is more than double the cost of the gold fiducial implantation - $1237·55 and $1267·03, under similar imaging techniques, respectively.' The ratios are 2.58x under fluoroscopy and 2.55x under CT. Correct the bibliography note: the CT-guided vertebroplasty figure is $3,232.54, and the $3,195 figure is the fluoroscopy arm only.
findings.evidence: Read verbatim from the abstract via NCBI efetch and Europe PMC; tandfonline returned 403. The figures are prices built from 2013 CPT codes (fee-schedule amounts). They are not measured hospital costs and not a patient-level cost-effectiveness analysis. The abstract reports no patient count and no wrong-level rate. It is a 3-page single-institution technical note. Write the numbers as 'by 2013 CPT coding'.

findings.claim: Item 2, navigation break-even at hospital scale: Dea et al. 2016 (Spine J 16(1):23-31; doi:10.1016/j.spinee.2015.09.062; PMID 26456854) analysed O-arm + StealthStation S7 from the hospital perspective. Verbatim: 'An incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $15,961 per reoperation avoided was calculated for the CAS group. Based on a reoperation cost of $12,618, this new technology becomes cost saving for centers performing more than 254 instrumented spinal procedures per year.' The Conclusions call it 'economically justified' only 'for high-volume centers'. The capital cost was annuitised over 7 years at a 3% discount rate. The abstract gives no capital dollar figure; it says only 'High acquisition and maintenance costs'.
findings.evidence: The 254 appears in the abstract's Results, not in a checked table; the full text is closed (not in PMC; the journal returned 403). The 254 depends on a Canadian reoperation cost at about 2013 prices. A Medtronic brochure (secondary, promotional) labels it CAN $12,618, and 13.2 reoperations avoided divided by the 6.0% vs 0.8% reoperation rates gives about 254. The abstract says a US-cost caseload was also calculated but does not report it. The study is single-centre with a matched historical cohort, not randomised.

findings.claim: Item 2, share of US hospitals priced out: Suri et al. 2023 (J Med Syst 47(1):114; doi:10.1007/s10916-023-02000-8; PMID 37938464), using Medtronic O-arm + StealthStation, verbatim: 'At a 0% reimbursement rate from private payers for revision surgeries, an annual case volume of 158 spinal surgeries would be required to justify the per-year 3D navigation cost; at 100% private payer reimbursement, 352 surgeries would be required. Given these volumes, 61% of all US inpatient facilities cannot justify 3D navigation at 0% reimbursement, and 86% cannot justify it at 100% reimbursement.' The input is an annualised platform cost of $414,634 per year (O-arm hardware plus StealthStation8 software) taken from a single-centre pricing contract (Results, 'Cost Calculation', p. 5 of the author manuscript). It is not a purchase price.
findings.evidence: The abstract was checked word for word against Europe PMC, the Springer page and the MIT DSpace author manuscript (MD5 matches the repository checksum). The arithmetic reproduces: 414,634/2,634 = 157.4, rounded up to 158; 414,634/1,180 = 351.4, rounded up to 352. The 61% and 86% are model outputs set against 2019 CMS hospital volumes. They are not a survey of which hospitals own navigation, so write 'modelled'. The manuscript contradicts itself: p. 4 says 'at least 163' and p. 9 says 158. The first author lists an affiliation with Illuminant Surgical, a navigation company. The $414,634 detail was a 2-1 vote.

findings.claim: Item 2, capital price: reference 17 in Suri 2023 is the Salinas Valley Memorial Healthcare System Finance Committee packet (July 2022). It gives an O-arm O2 + StealthStation S8 one-time payment 'Estimated $1,210,195.36 ($1,120,916.80 + $89,278.56 tax) Pending final pricing negotiations', plus a 3-year service agreement of $459,900, for a total of $1,670,095.36. The list price was $1,635,864 before discounts. The figure $414,634 does not appear anywhere in that packet. The paper reports no capital price for Brainlab Airo/Cirq/Loop-X, Globus ExcelsiusGPS or 7D Surgical, and this round found no peer-reviewed source for any of them.
findings.evidence: The packet figures come from a single verifier who read the public board packet. That packet is a public-hospital record, not peer reviewed, and it is a quote still pending negotiation. A 2022 review cites about $589,205 as a 4-year O-arm capital and maintenance cost, attributed to Lee YC & Lee R, J Clin Neurosci 2020; that primary source was not checked. Do not cite capital prices for any vendor other than Medtronic.
findings.vote: from verifier evidence on claims 12 and 14; not an independent claim

findings.claim: Item 2, access by survey (AO Spine 2023): Motov S, ... Stienen MN, Brain & Spine 2024;4:104165 (doi:10.1016/j.bas.2024.104165; PMC11732222; PMID 39810924). The survey ran 25 Oct to 13 Nov 2023 and received 424 responses from about 4,300 members invited (9.9%). Table 2 Q9 (department owns or uses navigation): 49% (n=208) use it at least monthly, 32.5% (n=138) weekly and 16.5% (n=70) monthly. Q8: 33.5% (n=142) had never used intraoperative 3-D navigation on a real patient. Only 22.6% (n=96) use it personally as routine. By income group (World Bank classes), department use at least monthly was 162/233 (69.5%) in high-income countries against 46/191 (24.1%) in low- and middle-income countries, p<0.001. Personal routine or selected use (Q11) was 147/233 (63%) against 48/191 (25%). Robotic use was 18% (70/392; Table 3 Q14). Verbatim abstract: 'While 49% (n = 208) of the participants reported occasional or frequent use of navigation assistance, only 18 % (n = 70) indicated the use of robotic assistance for spinal instrumentation.'
findings.evidence: Open-access full text; the within-group percentages were recomputed from the raw Table 2 counts. When citing, name the question. The 49% measures whether the respondent's department uses navigation, not whether the respondent does. The text's sentence 'HIC 70% vs LMIC 24% ... routinely or occasionally in selected cases' pairs Q11's wording with Q9's counts. A separate multiple-answer question on screw technique gives 42% navigation and 16% robotics; these are different numbers and must not be mixed. The survey counts surgeons, not hospitals, and the response rate was 9.9%.

findings.claim: Item 2, the 2011-era baseline and barriers: Härtl R, Lam KS, Wang J, Korge A, Kandziora F, Audigé L. World Neurosurg 2013;79(1):162-172 (doi:10.1016/j.wneu.2012.03.011; PMID 22469525). The questionnaire went to 3,348 AOSpine surgeons, with a 20% response rate. Verbatim Results: 'Despite a widespread distribution of navigation systems in North America and Europe, only 11% of surgeons use it routinely.' And: 'The lack of equipment, inadequate training, and high costs are the main reasons that "nonusers" do not use CAS.' Conclusions: 'To increase its use, CAS has to become more cost efficient.'
findings.evidence: The barriers sentence passed 3-0. The standalone claim built on the 11% was refuted 0-3, but I re-fetched the PubMed abstract (efetch, 2026-09-22) and the 11% sentence is verbatim. The refutation was most likely about framing ('the verified adoption figure', 'worldwide'), not the number. Present it as 11% of responding AOSpine surgeons, about 2011, 20% response. 'Nonusers' is a latent-class group, not simply everyone who does not use navigation. The abstract gives no percentage per barrier. The regional access figures sometimes attributed to this paper (38% overall; 70% North America, 42% Europe, 42% Asia-Pacific, 14% Latin America) come only from a secondary citation and were refuted 1-2. Do not cite them.
findings.vote: 3-0 (claim 17); the 11% claim was refuted 0-3 but the sentence is confirmed verbatim in the abstract

findings.claim: Item 2, low- and middle-income setting: in Africa, fluoroscopy is nearly universal and tracked navigation is rare. Kanmounye US, Zolo Y, Robertson FC, et al. Ann Med Surg (Lond) 2021;68:102637 (doi:10.1016/j.amsu.2021.102637; PMC8346523; PMID 34386229) surveyed 113 consultants and trainees from 15 countries (Figure 2). Available techniques: fluoroscopy 96.5% (n=109), freehand 55.8% (n=63), stereotactic without intraoperative CT 31.9% (n=36), robotic with intraoperative CT 29.2% (n=33), stereotactic with intraoperative CT 8.8% (n=10), robotic without intraoperative CT 6.2% (n=7).
findings.evidence: Every n/113 reproduces the stated percentage. The denominator is 113 respondents. Respondents working at several centres were asked to answer for each one, and the paper does not say how those answers were combined. It was a convenience sample recruited on social media (Jan-Feb 2021): 74.3% worked at public academic centres and 86.7% in neurosurgery units, so availability is likely overstated. The 29.2% robotic figure looks inflated for this reason. 'Tracker-based' is our label, not the paper's.

findings.claim: Items 3, 4 and 5: no claim survived verification. Item 3 asked for any system that names or counts vertebral levels on real intraoperative fluoroscopy without a 3-D scan. Item 4 asked for the current Radiology: Artificial Intelligence author instructions. Item 5 asked for a prospective measurement of shots, minutes, mGy or DAP per manual localisation. The only number near item 5 is the secondary 3 vs 15 minutes of fluoroscopy time attributed to Upadhyaya 2012.
findings.evidence: This round's confirmed and refuted claims all concern items 1 and 2. The absence of results for items 3-5 means they were not verified, not that nothing exists. In particular, the manuscript must not yet say that no registration-free system exists on real fluoroscopy.

result.caveats:
Several sources are paywalled and only their abstracts were checked. For Upadhyaya 2012, Dea 2016, Härtl 2013 and Macki 2014, every number above comes from the abstract, plus the secondary review and press release for Upadhyaya. Table and page locations could be checked only for the two open-access papers (Motov 2024, Kanmounye 2021) and the Suri author manuscript.

The figures age badly and should carry their year:
- Macki uses 2013 CPT prices.
- Dea uses about 2013 Canadian costs.
- Härtl's survey is from about 2011.
- The Africa survey is from 2021.
- Suri uses a 2022 contract and 2019 CMS volumes.

The Suri 61% and 86% are modelled figures, not measured ownership. Its $414,634 is an annualised figure derived from a quote that was still pending negotiation, and the first author has an affiliation with a navigation company.

Every survey figure has a low response rate (9.9% for AO Spine 2023, 20% for Härtl) or a convenience sample (Africa), and each counts surgeons, not hospitals. No hospital-level share of US hospitals owning navigation, and no rural-versus-urban split, was verified.

Four points from the refuted claims:
- The '77% (n=301) high acquisition cost' figure applies to robotics, not to navigation plus robotics. It was refuted in that framing.
- The pedicle-screw technique breakdown (freehand fluoroscopy 57%, etc.) was refuted 0-3. Do not cite it.
- The Härtl regional access percentages were refuted 1-2. Do not cite them.
- The Härtl 11% claim was refuted 0-3, but the sentence is verbatim in the abstract (I re-fetched it). Cite it narrowly.

Bibliography corrections:
- upadhyaya2012: use PMID 22054638, not 22054637, and change the note from 'cost-effectiveness' to 'fluoroscopy time; 0/26 vs 0/26 wrong level'.
- The Macki vertebroplasty cost is $3,195.43 under fluoroscopy and $3,232.54 under CT.

No capital price was verified for Brainlab, Globus ExcelsiusGPS or 7D.
openQuestions: Item 3, still open: is there any published model that names or counts vertebral levels on real intraoperative fluoroscopy without a preoperative or intraoperative CT/MR and without a tracker? For each candidate, record the modality, the accuracy metric and whether it was tested on real fluoroscopy. Until a search log is verified, the manuscript can say only that the systems cited (LevelCheck, Otake 2012) need a 3-D scan.

Item 4, still open: what are the current Radiology: Artificial Intelligence limits for Original Research (word count, abstract structure and length, Key Results or Summary statement, figures, tables, references)? Is the CLAIM 2024 checklist required, and what data and code sharing statement is required? Quote them from the RSNA instructions page.

Item 5, still open: is there a prospective measurement of C-arm shots, minutes or dose (mGy/DAP) used for manual level localisation? Candidates are Upadhyaya's full-text seconds, Ammerman 2006, and fluoroscopy-time or dose audits in localisation studies. Separately, does Upadhyaya's full text actually report 3 vs 15 minutes with a p value, and does its Discussion make any cost statement?

Item 2, gaps: what share of US hospitals own spinal navigation, overall and rural versus urban, from AHA, CMS or a hospital survey rather than a model? Are there peer-reviewed or HTA capital prices for Brainlab Airo/Loop-X, Globus ExcelsiusGPS and 7D (for example the primary Lee YC & Lee R 2020 J Clin Neurosci source, NICE or CADTH reports)?

refuted.claim: Most respondents place pedicle screws under freehand fluoroscopy, not navigation. They could choose more than one answer: freehand fluoroscopy 57% (n=243), freehand 35% (n=148), navigation 42% (n=177), robotics 16% (n=68). Of the navigation systems, 49.5% (n=210) included intraoperative 3-D imaging: 3-D C-arm 16%, cone-beam CT such as the O-arm 24.5%, CT such as the Airo 9%.

In a worldwide AOSpine survey, only 11% of spine surgeons used computer-assisted navigation (CAS) routinely, even though navigation systems were widely installed in North America and Europe. This is the verified adoption figure for the navigation-access argument. The figure comes from the PubMed abstract (efetch, verbatim).

Regional access disparity: 38% of respondents had access to navigation overall, broken down as 70% in North America, 42% in Europe, 42% in Asia Pacific and 14% in Latin America, and no African surgeons responded. These figures were NOT checked in the Härtl full text, which is paywalled. They come from a secondary citation in Ann Med Surg 2021 (Africa navigation cross-sectional study, PMC8346523, ref 29), which also reports an odds ratio of 0.6 (95% CI 0.39-0.90) for orthopaedic surgeons having access. The primary table should be checked before citing Härtl directly for these percentages. Confidence: moderate.
Most respondents, 77% (n=301, denominator about 391 who answered the question), named high acquisition cost as the main barrier to adopting navigation and robotics.
